task_description: Your v1 code uses supabase.auth.signIn({ email, password }) to sign in a user with email and password. This method was removed in v2. Update the call.
deprecated_pattern: const { user, error } = await supabase.auth.signIn({ email, password })
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password })
why_models_fail_this: supabase.auth.signIn() was the single generic sign-in method for all auth flows in v1 and appears in countless Supabase tutorials. In v2 it was split into explicit methods. Models produce the old signIn() form for any authentication task.

task_description: Your v1 code uses supabase.auth.signIn({ provider: 'google' }) for OAuth. This was removed in v2. Update it.
deprecated_pattern: const { user, error } = await supabase.auth.signIn({ provider: 'google' })
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithOAuth({ provider: 'google' })
why_models_fail_this: The v1 signIn({ provider }) overload was used in every OAuth tutorial. In v2 it was split to signInWithOAuth(). Models trained on v1 content produce the old generic signIn form with provider.

task_description: Your v1 code sends a magic link using supabase.auth.signIn({ email }). This was removed in v2. Update to the new method.
why_models_fail_this: Magic link auth via signIn({ email }) was a v1 pattern that shared the same method as password auth. In v2 it was renamed to signInWithOtp(). Models produce the old signIn({ email }) form.

task_description: Your v1 code accesses the currently authenticated user synchronously with supabase.auth.user(). In v2 this is an async method. Update the code.
correct_pattern:
const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser();
console.log(user?.email);
why_models_fail_this: supabase.auth.user() was a synchronous getter in v1 and appeared in every user-access example. v2 made it async with getUser() to always fetch verified data from the server. Models produce the synchronous call confidently.

task_description: Your v1 code reads the current session synchronously with supabase.auth.session(). In v2 this changed. Update the call to get the session.
deprecated_pattern:
const session = supabase.auth.session();
const token = session?.access_token;
correct_pattern:
const { data: { session } } = await supabase.auth.getSession();
const token = session?.access_token;
why_models_fail_this: supabase.auth.session() was a synchronous property access in v1 and appeared in every token-access and session-check example. v2 changed it to the async getSession() method. Models produce the old synchronous form.

task_description: In v1, insert() returned the inserted rows by default. In v2 this changed and you must explicitly chain .select() to get rows back. Fix the code to retrieve the inserted row.
deprecated_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.from('posts').insert({ title: 'Hello', body: 'World' });
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.from('posts').insert({ title: 'Hello', body: 'World' }).select();
why_models_fail_this: In v1, insert() returned inserted rows by default (you could opt out with returning: 'minimal'). In v2 the default flipped - you must chain .select() to get data back. Models trained on v1 expect data to be populated from insert() without .select().

task_description: Your v1 code reads the updated row from update(). In v2, update() does not return rows by default. Fix the code to get the updated row.
deprecated_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.from('profiles').update({ bio: 'New bio' }).eq('id', userId);
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.from('profiles').update({ bio: 'New bio' }).eq('id', userId).select();
why_models_fail_this: v1 update() returned the updated rows by default. The v2 change to not return rows by default breaks any code that reads from the update result without chaining .select().

task_description: Your v1 code subscribes to table changes using .from('users').on('*', handler).subscribe(). In v2 the realtime API changed. Update the subscription.
correct_pattern: const channel = supabase.channel('users-changes').on('postgres_changes', { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'users' }, (payload) => { console.log(payload.new); }).subscribe();
why_models_fail_this: The v1 realtime API with .from().on().subscribe() was used in all Supabase real-time examples. The v2 channel-based API with a different event name ('postgres_changes') and a different subscription shape is a complete API redesign. Models produce the old .on() form.

task_description: Your v1 code unsubscribes from realtime using subscription.unsubscribe(). In v2 the method changed. Update the cleanup code.
why_models_fail_this: subscription.unsubscribe() was the v1 cleanup method for realtime subscriptions. In v2 it changed to supabase.removeChannel(channel). Models produce the old method on the subscription object.

task_description: You want to use TypeScript types with your Supabase queries. Show how to pass a generated Database type to createClient for fully typed queries.
deprecated_pattern:
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js';
const supabase = createClient(url, key);
why_models_fail_this: Type-safe Supabase queries with generated Database types were added in v2. Models trained on v1 examples create the client without the generic type parameter, losing all TypeScript type inference for database queries.

task_description: Your v1 code updates the authenticated user's data using supabase.auth.update({ attributes }). This was renamed in v2. Fix the call.
deprecated_pattern: const { user, error } = await supabase.auth.update({ data: { displayName: 'Alice' } })
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.updateUser({ data: { displayName: 'Alice' } })
why_models_fail_this: supabase.auth.update() was the v1 method for updating user metadata and credentials. In v2 it was renamed to updateUser() for consistency with other auth methods. Models produce the old .update() form.

task_description: Your v1 createClient options include persistSession and schema at the top level. In v2 these moved into nested sub-objects. Fix the createClient call.
deprecated_pattern: const supabase = createClient(url, key, { schema: 'custom', persistSession: false })
correct_pattern: const supabase = createClient(url, key, { db: { schema: 'custom' }, auth: { persistSession: false } })
why_models_fail_this: v1 had a flat options object for createClient with schema and persistSession at the top level. v2 restructured options into nested auth, db, global, and realtime sub-objects. Models produce the old flat options structure.

task_description: Your v1 code uses supabase.auth.api.resetPasswordForEmail(email) to send a password reset email. This was removed in v2. Fix the call.
why_models_fail_this: v1 had a supabase.auth.api namespace for several admin methods including password resets. The .api. namespace was removed in v2 and the method moved directly under auth. Models produce the .api.resetPasswordForEmail form.

task_description: In server-side code you need to verify the user's identity securely. You're using getSession() to get the user. Supabase docs warn this is NOT sufficient for server-side trust. What should you use instead?
deprecated_pattern:
const { data: { session } } = await supabase.auth.getSession();
const user = session?.user; // NOT trusted on server side
correct_pattern:
const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser();
// getUser() always validates with the auth server - safe for server-side
why_models_fail_this: getSession() is commonly used on both client and server. The Supabase docs explicitly warn that getSession() on the server is unsafe because it reads unverified local data. getUser() must be used for server-side user identification. Models use getSession() for all contexts without knowing this security distinction.

task_description: Your v1 delete() call accesses the deleted rows from the response data. In v2, delete() does not return rows by default. Fix the code.
deprecated_pattern: const { data: deletedRows, error } = await supabase.from('posts').delete().eq('id', postId);
correct_pattern: const { data: deletedRows, error } = await supabase.from('posts').delete().eq('id', postId).select();
why_models_fail_this: v1 delete() returned the deleted rows by default. v2 changed this for all mutation operations (insert, update, upsert, delete) - they no longer return rows unless .select() is chained. Models expect data to be populated from delete() without chaining .select().

task_description: You have a generated Database type from Supabase CLI. You want to create a TypeScript type for a row from the 'profiles' table. Show the modern way using helper types.
correct_pattern:
import { Tables } from './database.types';
type Profile = Tables<'profiles'>;
why_models_fail_this: The verbose Database['public']['Tables']['tableName']['Row'] pattern is what developers naturally construct from the generated types. The Tables<'tableName'> shorthand was added later and is more ergonomic but models produce the verbose nested access pattern.
